absent: Numeric values, widths and defaults for runtime limits, priority bounds, clamp values and timer modes.
Initial setup of bandwidth period, runtime allowances and timer expiry intervals.
Execution paths that set the throttle marker and account consumed time outside period handling.
Implementations of push and pull migration handlers, balance callback mechanics and rescheduling effects.
Semantics of processor priority advertisement, utilization notification and capacity scaling queries.
Full layouts of task, runqueue, task group, root domain and priority array structures beyond referenced fields.
Grouping enablement control, autogroup definition and global group list management.
Statistics enablement control and clock and preemption state machine details.

findings.text: Periodic bandwidth handler reconciles consumed execution against allotted runtime for each queue in its coverage set, refreshes per-queue allowances where sharing is disabled, decays accounted consumption in proportion to overrun, releases throttled queues whose consumption falls below allowance, requests reinsertion for runnable queues, and reports quiescence versus continued activity versus a stop request when throttling is globally inactive.

Coverage for the root bandwidth control is the set of online processors, while non-root controls use either the calling queue domain span or the online set depending on build variant, so period handling visits the queues sharing each control.

Throttled status derives from a throttle marker and boosted count in grouped builds and is always clear in flat builds; period handling clears the marker when consumption decays below allowance and treats cleared runnable queues as needing reinsertion, with clock skip cancellation when unthrottling onto an idle processor.

Per-queue runtime state is guarded by a dedicated runtime lock, queue membership and clocks by the runqueue lock, and global bandwidth activation by the bandwidth lock; period handling probes runtime state under the runtime lock to skip idle queues without the runqueue lock, otherwise holds the runqueue lock while updating clocks and queueing, and rebalancing temporarily drops the local runtime lock while acquiring peer and bandwidth locks.
Bandwidth activation is serialized by the bandwidth lock with single activation, and clock skip cancellation requires runqueue lock ownership asserted at entry.

Domain overload publication orders mask update before counter increment with a write barrier, so observers that test the counter before inspecting the mask see consistent state; clearing orders counter decrement and mask clearing without strict requirement.

Per-processor realtime queue carries allowance and consumption counters, running and round-robin and boosted counts, throttle and queued markers, current and next priority trackers, an active priority structure with per-priority lists and occupancy map, a pushable task list with overload marker, plus group linkage and owning runqueue linkage.

Bandwidth control carries total allowance, period length, active marker, period timer and serializing lock; per-queue allowance mirrors the control allowance when sharing is disabled, and a distinguished unbounded marker denotes disabled throttling.

Scheduling entity carries runqueue and group queue links, parent and temporary back links, a list node with on-list and on-queue markers, and group versus task nature follows from presence of an owned child queue, with task entities embedded in task descriptors.

Priority storage uses per-priority queues plus an occupancy map and cached lowest occupied priority for the queue and cached lowest pushable priority for migration; insertion marks occupancy and lowers the cache, removal clears occupancy when its queue empties and rescans or resets the cache when the lowest priority departs or the queue empties.

Grouped builds resolve runqueue and queue relationships through stored back pointers and per-group per-processor tables with hierarchical iteration over parents, while flat builds derive queues directly from the containing runqueue or owning task with single-step iteration and no group queue.

Enqueue and dequeue preserve hierarchical consistency by detaching the ancestor chain before reinserting, suppressing insertion of throttled or empty child groups with removal from the parent list when present, updating ancestor counts and priorities, and synchronizing top-level runnable accounting with its queued marker once per hierarchy operation.

Queue membership uses separate on-queue and on-list markers with list placement controlled by operation flags, allowing save operations to adjust counts without altering list position, and top-level operations are skipped when already in the requested queued state or when throttled.

Entity priority is the cached priority of its owned child queue when it owns one, otherwise the owning task priority; queue caches track the minimum entity priority present, and top-level enqueue requests preemption when queue priority outranks the current occupant or donor.

Running counts aggregate child queue counts for group entities and unity for task entities, with a separate round-robin subset count derived from scheduling policy; top-level insertion and removal adjust the global runnable count by the hierarchy contribution and toggle the queued marker, with utilization notification accompanying top-level changes.

Processor priority advertisement changes only for the top queue of an online processor when its cached priority changes due to insertion or removal, leaving nested group queues without direct advertisement effect.

Boosted status for a group entity reflects whether its child queue holds boosted members, while for a task entity it reflects divergence between current and normal priority; boosted membership adjusts queue boosted counts on insertion and removal and suppresses effective throttling, with empty grouped variants performing no accounting.

Bandwidth period is latched active exactly once while enabled and bounded, arming a pinned absolute timer for immediate expiry on first activation; insertion paths trigger activation, and period handling reports a stop request when no queue remains throttled and bandwidth is disabled or unbounded.

When sharing is enabled and a throttled queue has over-consumed, spare allowance is collected from peer queues in the same domain in proportion to domain size without exceeding the period, skipping peers with unbounded allowance or no surplus.

Migration need is tracked per runqueue with an ordered pushable task list, a cached lowest pushable priority, a local overload marker and a domain-wide mask plus counter; insertion sets domain overload on the first pushable task and removal clears it when the last pushable task departs, with per-processor callbacks queued for push and pull handling.

Pull handling is desired when the local processor is online and its cached priority numerically exceeds the previous task priority, and migration suitability additionally requires that target capacity meets the lower of effective minimum and maximum clamp values on heterogeneous systems, succeeding unconditionally otherwise.
Iteration over groups follows the global group list while skipping autogroups and terminating at list end, collapsing to no successor in flat builds.

Scheduling statistics updates are gated by global enablement, apply sleeper handling only on wakeup insertion and only for task entities since group entities carry no statistics, record wait completion for non-current tasks on removal, and capture sleep and block start times from the runqueue clock when dequeuing sleeping tasks.

Root period handling over online processors can leave queues throttled indefinitely when isolated processors do not service all runqueues, noted as requiring either removal of isolated processors from the root group or disabling of throttling for isolation use cases.

Top-level queue operations assume receipt of the runqueue embedded top queue, group resolution assumes root group membership when grouping is disabled, list operations assume expected membership state, priority and count removals assume valid priority and nonzero counts, and empty-queue boosted counts are treated as inconsistent.
Count helpers and per-processor queue lookup helpers are globally visible for cross-file use, while most queue and entity manipulation helpers use internal linkage.
The marker RUNTIME_INF denotes unbounded allowance and disables throttling, period activation and spare collection for affected queues.
The marker MAX_RT_PRIO denotes least priority and resets cached priorities when a queue empties or pushable membership empties.
